title: What to watch at the open
text: Markets are closed on weekends, so these prices are still Friday's close. That day was rough: the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 3.5% to $690.49 and the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 1.8% to $755.72. When trading opens today, watch whether tech keeps sliding or steadies. A calm open does not mean the worry is gone, and a big drop does not mean a crash. Prices move on mood as well as facts. This is for learning, not advice.

title: Chip makers took the biggest hit
text: AMD fell 10.9% to $504.80, TSMC fell 5.9%, Broadcom fell 5.5% and Vertiv fell 5.5%. These companies sell parts and equipment for AI, so they often move together. The AI giants (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta) fell a smaller 1.4% to 1.6%.

title: Fed meeting ahead in December
text: The Fed kept interest rates unchanged on October 28, but two members voted to raise them. When rates may go up, investors often pay less for fast-growing tech companies, because money in safe places pays more. The next Fed meeting is in December.

title: Lilly rose while tech fell
text: Eli Lilly gained 3.2% to $1,417.54, close to its 52 week high of $1,449.68, after raising its yearly sales forecast. Health care and tech often move differently, which is one reason people mix industries.

title: Lesson 32: What is the 10 year Treasury yield?
text: When the US government borrows money, it sells bonds called Treasuries. The 10 year Treasury yield is the yearly interest the government pays on a bond that lasts 10 years. People watch it because it works like a base price for money. When the yield goes up, safe bonds look more attractive, and investors may pay less for stocks, especially fast-growing tech companies whose profits come far in the future. On our board, the monthly average yield rose from about 4.3% in April to 4.99% in September. A rising yield does not mean stocks must fall, but it is one reason prices can swing.
